SEC-01   /   ENGINEERING REFERENCE
Purpose and interpretation

Scope of the engineering reference

1.1 Document purpose

This reference defines the publicly observable behavior of the fictional Brahmastra monitoring system. It describes 
subsystem roles, registered telemetry semantics, phase identifiers, timestamp conventions, and evidence requirements for 
interpreting a synthetic mission record. Its purpose is reproducible engineering-style analysis over multiple linked sources.

1.2 System boundaries

Brahmastra is represented as a logical, non-operational digital twin. It has fourteen monitored subsystem domains and a 
fixed seven-phase observation timeline. The terms “stage,” “actuator,” and “safety” identify software-visible states; they do 
not establish mechanical architectures, control laws, physical thresholds, or operational procedures.

EXPLICIT EXCLUSIONS  No targeting, propulsion design, guidance, flight control, destructive mechanisms, weapon 
effectiveness, real-world operating envelopes, or deployment instructions are defined in this document.

1.3 Status of statements

Specification statements

Subsystem identifiers, ownership, telemetry types, valid domains, phase identifiers and logical consistency rules are treated 
as the governing vocabulary for this version. A valid observation may be nominal, degraded, missing, late, contradictory, or 
of uncertain quality.

Illustrative observation records

Screenshots and time-series panels are examples from known synthetic runs. They are not additional specifications, nor 
may their visual annotations be used to infer undocumented operating limits.

Unresolved items

SEC-02   /   ENGINEERING REFERENCE
System overview

Conceptual physical view and monitoring focus

FIG-01 — Conceptual exterior zones; not a dimensioned hardware layout

Brahmastra provides a consistent frame for interpreting telemetry, subsystem health and event sequencing. The exterior 
illustration identifies plausible-looking regions solely to orient a human reader. The depiction is not a parts list or a 
mechanical specification.

2.1 What the system measures

The canonical system measures configuration validity, normalized supply and thermal indicators, acquisition and 
communications quality, mission supervisory state, abstract stage-event status, environmental observations, safety-state 
evidence, actuator status and logger behavior.

2.2 What the system does not infer

A labeled exterior region is not proof of an internal wiring route or a particular physical component. Analysts should identify a 
subsystem only through its canonical ID, documented responsibility, and associated telemetry channels.

SEC-02   /   ENGINEERING REFERENCE
Dependency interpretation

Cross-subsystem evidence relationships

FIG-03 — Dependency network, including upstream and downstream observability

2.4 Interpreting a correlated warning sequence

A warning recorded in several subsystems need not imply several unrelated faults. Begin with the documented dependency 
graph, then compare onset times and the quality of each observation. A shared upstream indicator can provide a candidate 
explanation, but the graph alone cannot establish causality.

Example of the distinction

PWR → THM is a declared monitoring dependency. If a power-health change is observed before a thermal warning, the 
time sequence and relationship support further investigation. They do not by themselves prove that the first observation 
physically caused the second.

EVIDENCE STANDARD  Treat any dependency-based explanation as a hypothesis until supported by independent 
channel values, event times, and logger integrity.

Subsystem reference / group A

3.1 CFG — Configuration Management

CFG identifies the synthetic operating profile and revision, and exposes the configuration-integrity status used by readiness 
checks. The principal observation is whether the reported revision and profile remain consistent across an individual run. A 
profile change is metadata; it is not a real physical vehicle configuration instruction.

3.2 SUP — Mission Supervisor

SUP reports the high-level state IDLE, READY, ACTIVE, SAFE or ARCHIVED, the monitoring mode NORMAL, CAUTION 
or RECOVERY, heartbeat age and cumulative fault observations. The state is an observed supervisory classification rather 
than an operational command interface.

3.3 SEQ — Phase Sequencer

SEQ exposes the currently reported major phase and subphase plus pending-state and delay indicators. Its sequence 
follows the canonical phase model in SEC-05 for nominal runs. Where a report is late, an independent monitor or log record 
can preserve a different view of the same episode.

Primary reading pattern

Read CFG before interpreting readiness. Read SUP and SEQ together when a phase label appears inconsistent. Confirm 
the reported phase with the event log rather than interpreting a single state sample in isolation.

3.4 PWR — Power Monitoring

PWR reports normalized bus level, load, and health margin, together with an explicit fault indicator. A lower margin may 
accompany degraded health without implying any calibrated bus voltage. A valid fault interpretation requires checking the 
declared PWR flag and related observations rather than inventing a threshold from the plot.

3.5 THM — Thermal Monitoring

THM exposes normalized enclosure and payload/electronics temperature indicators. The delta channel is defined as core 
minus payload. THM warning is a recorded monitoring assessment; it is not a thermal-engineering shutdown condition.

3.6 CLK — Time Synchronization

CLK reports offset in milliseconds, lock state, and a cumulative resynchronization counter. Its role is especially important 
when apparent event ordering conflicts with receipt times. A clock resynchronization must be recorded explicitly; the source 
sample order is not silently rewritten.

DERIVED SIGNAL  For each valid source row, thm_delta_pu = thm_core_temp_pu − thm_payload_temp_pu, subject only 
to documented numeric rounding.

3.7 DAQ — Data Acquisition

DAQ characterizes source sampling frequency, missing source observations, data quality and buffer utilization. The nominal 
rate is 2 Hz, corresponding to one source slot every 0.5 seconds. Missing-source counters represent acquisition gaps, not 
communication delivery loss.

3.8 COM — Communications Monitoring

COM represents the delivery link: connection status, loss percentage, latency and elapsed interruption. COM degradation is 
compatible with healthy source acquisition. Conversely, good delivery does not guarantee that the measurements originated 
correctly.

3.9 LOG — Event Logger

LOG preserves a sequence counter, integrity flag and backlog depth. Backlog indicates delayed event processing. Evidence 
may include an event source timestamp, its later received timestamp, and a sequence number that permits reconstruction 
after delivery delay.

DO NOT CONFLATE  DAQ missing samples, COM packet delivery loss, and LOG backlog are three different conditions. 
They require different evidence even when a dashboard shows a similar “missing data” symptom.

3.10 HLT — Health Aggregation

HLT consolidates subsystem warnings into the canonical NOMINAL, WARNING, DEGRADED and UNKNOWN 
classifications. hlt_warning_count is an observed count; hlt_degraded is a Boolean indicator. Both must be reconciled with 
the underlying warning evidence.

3.11 STG — Stage Event Monitor

STG is an abstract evidence source for the phase-transition observation. Values NOT_APPLICABLE, PENDING, 
CONFIRMED and UNKNOWN refer to monitoring records only. No physical separation, ignition or motion mechanism is 
described.

3.12 ACT — Actuator Status Monitor

ACT records generic component response states, reported acknowledgement lag and a fault indication. No control law, 
actuation dynamics, or mechanism geometry is modeled.

3.13 SAF — Safety State Monitor

SAF reports the software monitoring classification CHECKING, READY, MONITORING, SAFE or UNKNOWN, the software 
interlock status, and cumulative state-change observations. “SAFE” is a synthetic report; it is not proof of physical safing.

classifications. hlt_warning_count is an observed count; hlt_degraded is a Boolean indicator. Both must be reconciled with

STG is an abstract evidence source for the phase-transition observation. Values NOT_APPLICABLE, PENDING,

interlock status, and cumulative state-change observations. “SAFE” is a synthetic report; it is not proof of physical safing.

SEC-04   /   ENGINEERING REFERENCE
Telemetry interpretation rules

Common schema for all forty-eight channels

4.1 Row structure and source times

Each CSV row is a source observation slot identified by public run ID, sample index, mission elapsed seconds and source 
time. Separate received-time and delivery-state fields describe reporting. The nominal schedule contains 1,800 source slots 
over [0, 900) seconds at 2 Hz. A run with source loss can contain fewer observed rows.

Metadata field
Meaning

run_id
Public, scenario-neutral identifier

sample_index
Source-slot index; use to detect dropped slots

mission_elapsed_s
Run-relative time, seconds

source_time_utc
Acquisition/observation timestamp

received_time_utc
Report/delivery timestamp

delivery_state
Delivery observation; separate from source sampling

4.2 Channel types

F = floating-point quantity; I = integer counter; B = Boolean status; E = enumerated state; S = string identifier. Allowed 
domains are syntax constraints, not nominal operating envelopes. An in-domain value may still be anomalous for its context.

4.3 Missingness and counters

Do not interpolate missing Boolean or enumerated event states as if they were continuous signals. Cumulative counters are 
evaluated within a defined clock epoch. Observations with missing source samples or delayed receipt should preserve their 
quality and timing evidence.

IMPORTANT  The following four pages reproduce all 48 canonical channel definitions. Every channel is recorded at a 
nominal 2 Hz; any sparse arrival or missing slot must be interpreted through the data-quality fields.

Classification vocabulary without invented guards

FIG-06 — Health-classification and supporting-evidence relationships

6.1 Health classifications

NOMINAL indicates that no relevant warning evidence has been reported in the aggregate. WARNING indicates active 
warning evidence; DEGRADED indicates a stronger aggregate health condition. UNKNOWN reflects insufficient or 
unreliable status evidence. These categories describe observations, not commands.

6.2 Known limitation of this revision

The canonical registry does not yet specify a complete state-transition graph, hysteresis, or explicit guard thresholds for 
every health transition. The figure is therefore a status model, not a deterministic transition diagram. Rules R06 and R07 
constrain evidence consistency, not closed-loop operation.
